description: The shapes data takes in memory: arrays, linked chains, stacks and queues, hash tables, trees, and graphs, plus the abstract types they implement and the memory they live in.

concepts.title: Data Structures
concepts.summary: How data is arranged in memory so the things you do most, finding, adding, and removing, stay fast. The same information in a different shape can be thousands of times quicker or slower to use, which makes choosing the shape half of programming.

concepts.title: Arrays
concepts.summary: Items stored side by side in memory and reached by position. Because the address of item n is simple arithmetic, any element is read in the same tiny time, which makes arrays the default container and the base of most other structures.

concepts.title: Dynamic Arrays
concepts.summary: An array that grows: when it fills, it allocates one twice as big and copies across. Most appends are nearly free and an occasional one is expensive, which averages out to constant time. Python lists and C++ vectors work this way.

concepts.title: Strings
concepts.summary: Text stored as a sequence of characters. Simple in principle, full of choices in practice: how characters are encoded, whether a string can be changed in place, and how long ones are compared, joined, and searched without wasteful copying.

concepts.title: Locality
concepts.summary: Programs tend to reuse data they just used and data stored next to it. Processors bet on this by fetching memory in blocks and caching it, which is why scanning an array is far faster than following pointers between scattered nodes.

concepts.title: Linked Lists
concepts.summary: A chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next. Inserting or removing in the middle only rewires pointers, with no shuffling of the rest, but reaching item number n means walking from the start.

concepts.title: Doubly Linked Lists
concepts.summary: A linked list where each node points both forward and back. You can walk either way and remove a node when you hold only that node, at the price of an extra pointer per item. Browser history and undo lists use the idea.

concepts.title: Skip Lists
concepts.summary: A linked list with express lanes: extra layers of pointers, built by coin flips, let a search skip over many items at once. It behaves like a balanced tree with much simpler code, and some databases use it to keep data sorted.

concepts.title: Pointers
concepts.summary: A value that is the address of something else in memory. Pointers make linked structures possible and let programs share data without copying it, and they are also the source of some of the most notorious bugs and security holes.

concepts.title: Memory Management
concepts.summary: Deciding who owns which bytes and when they are handed back. Manual allocation is fast and easy to get wrong; garbage collection and ownership rules trade some speed or freedom for safety. Every long-running program has to solve it.

concepts.title: Garbage Collection
concepts.summary: Automatic reclaiming of memory that nothing can reach anymore. The runtime periodically finds what is still in use and frees the rest, sparing programmers from freeing by hand, in exchange for occasional pauses and some extra memory.

concepts.title: Memory Leaks
concepts.summary: Memory a program keeps holding after it has stopped needing it. Usage creeps up until the machine slows or the process is killed. Forgotten references, unclosed resources, and ever-growing caches are the usual causes.

concepts.title: Stacks
concepts.summary: Last in, first out, like a pile of plates: you only touch the top. Push, pop, and peek are all instant. Undo history, bracket matching, and the way a program remembers where to return after each function call are all stacks.

concepts.title: The Call Stack
concepts.summary: The stack a running program uses to track function calls. Each call pushes a frame holding its arguments and where to return; finishing pops it. It is why recursion works, and why runaway recursion ends in a stack overflow.

concepts.title: Stack Overflow
concepts.summary: What happens when a program pushes more onto its call stack than the space allows, usually through recursion that never stops. The program crashes, and related bugs that overwrite data on the stack have long been a route for attackers.

concepts.title: Reverse Polish
concepts.summary: Writing an operator after its operands, so 3 4 + means 3 plus 4. It needs no brackets and no precedence rules: read left to right, push numbers on a stack, and let each operator take what it needs. Calculators and compilers use it.

concepts.title: Queues
concepts.summary: First in, first out, like a line at a shop: add at the back, take from the front. Print jobs, network buffers, and tasks waiting for a worker are queues, and the structure itself enforces fairness.

concepts.title: Priority Queues
concepts.summary: A queue where the most urgent item leaves first, not the oldest. Operating system schedulers, event simulations, and shortest-path searches all need 'give me the best one next', and it is usually built on a heap.

concepts.title: Deques
concepts.summary: A double-ended queue: add or remove at either end in constant time. It works as a stack, a queue, or both, and suits sliding windows, undo and redo, and work-stealing schedulers.

concepts.title: Circular Buffers
concepts.summary: A fixed-size array treated as a loop: when the write position reaches the end, it wraps to the start and overwrites the oldest. Audio streams, keyboard input, and log tails use it because it never allocates or shifts.

concepts.title: Message Queues
concepts.summary: A queue that sits between programs so one can hand work to another without waiting for it. Producers add messages, consumers take them at their own pace, and the queue absorbs bursts and survives restarts.

concepts.title: Producer–Consumer
concepts.summary: A classic coordination problem: some workers produce items, others consume them, and a shared buffer sits between. The trick is to stop producers overfilling it and consumers reading it empty, without wasting time waiting.

concepts.title: Hash Tables
concepts.summary: Turn a key into a number and use the number as an index. Lookup, insert, and delete become nearly instant on average, at the price of no useful ordering and the need to handle two keys landing in the same slot.

concepts.title: Hash Functions
concepts.summary: A function that maps any input to a fixed-size number, scrambling it so similar inputs land far apart. For tables it needs to be fast and evenly spread; for security it must also be impossible to reverse or to collide on purpose.

concepts.title: Collisions
concepts.summary: When two different keys hash to the same slot. Tables handle it by chaining items in a short list per slot or by probing for the next free one. How well they cope decides whether lookups stay instant or slow to a crawl.

concepts.title: Bloom Filters
concepts.summary: A tiny structure that answers 'have I seen this?' with either 'definitely not' or 'probably'. It uses several hash functions and a bit array, never forgets an item, and trades a small false-positive rate for enormous savings in memory.

concepts.title: Consistent Hashing
concepts.summary: A way of spreading keys over servers so that adding or removing one moves only a small share of them. Caches, databases, and content networks use it so that growing a cluster does not reshuffle everything.

concepts.title: Trees
concepts.summary: Nodes with children, one root, and no loops: file systems, web pages, organization charts. Halving the search at each level lets a well-shaped tree find things in a handful of steps even among millions.

concepts.title: Binary Trees
concepts.summary: A tree where every node has at most two children, left and right. Simple as it is, it gives rise to search trees, heaps, expression trees, and the decision trees behind much of machine learning.

concepts.title: Binary Search Trees
concepts.summary: A binary tree kept in order: everything on the left of a node is smaller, everything on the right larger. Searching goes left or right at each node, halving the work, as long as the tree stays balanced.

concepts.title: Balanced Trees
concepts.summary: Search trees that rearrange themselves after each change so no branch grows much longer than the others. That guarantees searches in steps proportional to the logarithm of the size, even for the worst possible order of input.

concepts.title: AVL Trees
concepts.summary: The first self-balancing search tree, from 1962. Each node tracks the height difference of its subtrees and rotates when it exceeds one. Strictly balanced, so lookups are fast, at the cost of a few more rotations on updates.

concepts.title: Red–Black Trees
concepts.summary: A balanced tree that colors nodes red or black and follows a few simple rules to stay roughly even. Looser than AVL trees, so updates need fewer rotations, and it sits inside the ordered maps of many standard libraries.

concepts.title: Tree Rotations
concepts.summary: A local rearrangement that changes which node is on top of a small subtree while keeping the left-to-right order intact. Rotations are the basic move balanced trees use to repair themselves after an insert or delete.

concepts.title: B-Trees
concepts.summary: A wide, shallow balanced tree where each node holds many keys, sized to fit a disk page. Fewer levels means fewer slow reads, so B-trees sit underneath most databases and file systems.

concepts.title: Tries
concepts.summary: A tree spelled out letter by letter: each step down follows one character, so words with the same beginning share a path. Autocomplete, spell checkers, and IP routing tables lean on them.

concepts.title: Heaps
concepts.summary: A tree in which every parent outranks its children, so the smallest or largest is always at the top. It is the standard engine behind priority queues, and it packs neatly into a plain array with no pointers.

concepts.title: Segment Trees
concepts.summary: A tree that stores a summary, such as a sum or minimum, for every range of an array. It answers 'what is the total from here to there?' and updates single items, both in logarithmic time.

concepts.title: Tree Traversal
concepts.summary: Visiting every node in a systematic order: depth first, going before, between, or after the children, or level by level. The order you choose determines what you can compute along the way.

concepts.title: k-d Trees
concepts.summary: A tree that splits space one dimension at a time, so points in a plane or higher dimensions can be searched by region. Its main job is finding nearest neighbors without checking every point.

concepts.title: Graphs
concepts.summary: Things and the connections between them: dots and lines. Maps, social networks, the web, dependency lists, and the internet itself are graphs, which makes them the general language for anything that is related to something else.

concepts.title: Adjacency Lists
concepts.summary: Store a graph by giving each node a list of its neighbors. It uses space in proportion to the connections that actually exist, so it suits the sparse graphs of the real world: roads, links, friendships.

concepts.title: Adjacency Matrices
concepts.summary: Store a graph as a grid where entry (i, j) says whether i connects to j. Checking a connection is instant, but the grid grows with the square of the number of nodes, so it suits small or dense graphs.

concepts.title: Directed Graphs
concepts.summary: Graphs whose connections have a direction, like one-way streets, links between web pages, or 'follows' on social media. Who points to whom matters, and reachability is no longer symmetric.

concepts.title: Acyclic Graphs
concepts.summary: A directed graph with no way to follow the arrows back to where you started. It describes dependencies that can be ordered: build steps, course prerequisites, spreadsheets, and the history of a Git repository.

concepts.title: Union-Find
concepts.summary: A structure that tracks which items belong to the same group and can merge groups, both in nearly constant time. It answers 'are these two connected?' quickly and powers algorithms such as Kruskal's spanning tree.

concepts.title: Abstract Data Types
concepts.summary: A description of what a structure does without saying how: a list, a set, a map are defined by their operations. The same interface can be backed by an array, a tree, or a hash table, and the code using it need not care.

concepts.title: Lists
concepts.summary: An ordered collection you can add to, read from, and remove from by position. It is the abstract idea behind arrays and linked lists, and which one to use depends on what you do most often.

concepts.title: Sets
concepts.summary: A collection with no duplicates and no order, where the question is 'is this in it?'. Backed by a hash table or a balanced tree, it supports union, intersection, and difference, straight out of set theory.

concepts.title: Maps
concepts.summary: A collection of key–value pairs, where you look things up by name rather than position. Called a map, dictionary, or object depending on the language, and usually built on a hash table or a balanced tree.

concepts.title: Iterators
concepts.summary: A way of walking through a collection one item at a time without knowing how it is stored. The same loop then works over an array, a tree, a file, or an endless stream, which is much of what makes code reusable.

concepts.title: Graph Theory
concepts.summary: The mathematics of dots and lines. It began with an argument about crossing bridges and now underlies networks, scheduling, routing, and chemistry, since so many questions reduce to who is connected to whom.

concepts.title: Königsberg Bridges
concepts.summary: Seven bridges joined the parts of a Prussian city, and its residents wondered whether you could cross each exactly once. Euler showed in 1736 that you cannot, and in doing so founded graph theory.

concepts.title: Graph Coloring
concepts.summary: Give every node a color so that connected nodes never match, using as few colors as possible. It schedules exams, allocates registers in compilers, and assigns radio frequencies; the four-color theorem is its map version.

concepts.title: Small Worlds
concepts.summary: Networks where most nodes are not neighbors but any two are linked by a short chain, like six degrees of separation. Social ties, brain wiring, and the web all show it, and it explains why news and disease spread so fast.
